title: The System Design Interview
objectives: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.
Answer: What is graded in a design round?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Interviewers grade how you think, not a single right diagram. They watch for: clarifying scope, sensible numbers, a clean high-level design, a deep dive into one hard part, and honest trade-offs.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Clarify requirements” to “Trade-offs & wrap-up”, via “Estimate scale”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Jumping straight into Kafka and microservices before asking what the product does. Spend roughly the first five minutes on requirements; the interviewer may steer you sooner.

cards.title: Worked example: the first five minutes
cards.body: Interviewer: “Design a URL shortener.” Good clarifying questions: Who creates links, and roughly how many per day? Do links expire? Custom aliases? Is click analytics in scope? A strong opening answer: “I’ll assume 100M new links a month, about 100 reads per write, redirects under 50 ms, links never expire, analytics out of scope. Let me size that before drawing anything.”

questions.prompt: What should you do in the first five minutes?
questions.explanation: Scope first. Every later decision depends on what the system must do and at what scale.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a typical design interview.
questions.explanation: Requirements drive estimates, estimates drive design, and the deep dive validates it.

questions.prompt: What is graded in a design round?

choices.label: Peak traffic ≈ 2–10× average; spikier for events.

title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
objectives: Turn users into QPS, storage and bandwidth with rounded math: 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: QPS = DAU × actions per user ÷ 86,400. Peak ≈ 2–10× average. Storage = writes/day × object size × retention. Round aggressively; the order of magnitude matters.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Turn users into QPS, storage and bandwidth with rounded math: 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “DAU” to “× peak factor”, via “× actions/user”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Forgetting the peak factor. India traffic is spiky: cricket finals, Big Billion Days, Tatkal at 10 AM.

questions.prompt: 10M DAU, each makes 10 requests/day. Roughly what is average QPS?
A chat app has 50M DAU sending 40 messages/day each. Estimate average messages per second (answer in K/s).
assumptions: Use rounded daily volume ÷ 86,400 unless stated otherwise.

title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers
objectives: Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Vertical scaling is simple but hits a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, a load balancer and partitioned data. It adds capacity, and it only adds availability if the copies fail independently and traffic is routed away from dead ones (health checks, no shared single database). Gains are rarely linear: shared state, coordination and hot keys eat into them.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “One server” to “N servers (horizontal)”, via “Bigger server (vertical)”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Saying "just add servers" while keeping session state in server memory. Stateless first, then scale out.

questions.prompt: What must be true before app servers can scale horizontally easily?
questions.explanation: If any server can serve any request, you can add servers freely.

choices.label: Vertical scaling → Needs a load balancer

questions.explanation: Horizontal growth depends on removing per-server state.

title: OSI & TCP/IP
objectives: Place HTTP, TLS, TCP/UDP and IP in the right layer
Explain what a TCP handshake costs a request
Choose TCP or UDP for a given workload

cards.title: Why layers matter
cards.body: Interviewers rarely ask for all seven OSI layers. They ask which layer a component works at: an L4 load balancer sees IPs and ports, an L7 one sees HTTP paths and headers. Knowing the layer tells you what a box can and cannot do.

cards.title: The four layers you actually use
cards.body: Application (HTTP, gRPC, DNS) → Transport (TCP, UDP) → Internet (IP) → Link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). TCP gives ordered, reliable byte streams with retransmits; UDP gives fire-and-forget datagrams with no ordering.

cards.title: A new HTTPS connection
cards.body: 5 steps from “DNS lookup” to “Response”, via “TCP handshake (1 RTT)”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Ignoring round trips. From Mumbai to a us-east server one RTT is roughly 200 ms, so a cold HTTPS connection spends about 400 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive, connection pooling and edge termination exist to avoid paying that on every request.

questions.prompt: A live cricket score widget sends tiny updates every second; a lost update is fine because the next one replaces it. Which transport fits best?

choices.label: TCP, because every packet must arrive in order
UDP (or a UDP-based protocol like QUIC)

questions.explanation: Stale updates are worthless, so retransmitting them adds latency for nothing. UDP-based transports avoid head-of-line blocking. TCP would work, but it is not the best fit.

questions.prompt: Where does TLS sit in a typical HTTPS request?

choices.label: Between TCP and HTTP: it encrypts the byte stream TCP carries
Below IP, inside the network card

questions.explanation: TLS runs on top of TCP and below HTTP. QUIC (HTTP/3) folds transport and TLS together over UDP.

questions.prompt: Order what happens before the first byte of a brand-new HTTPS request.
questions.explanation: Name resolution, then the transport connection, then encryption, then the request itself.

flashcards.front: Which transport gives ordered, reliable delivery?
flashcards.back: TCP. UDP gives unordered datagrams with no retransmits.

flashcards.front: What does an L4 load balancer see?
flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.
Each new HTTPS connection pays TCP + TLS round trips before the first byte.

title: TCP vs UDP
objectives: HTTP is request/response over TCP; HTTPS adds TLS for encryption, integrity and server identity.
Answer: Where is TLS usually terminated?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: TLS handshake negotiates keys using certificates. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, HTTP/3 runs on QUIC (UDP) to avoid head-of-line blocking.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: HTTP is request/response over TCP; HTTPS adds TLS for encryption, integrity and server identity.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “TCP handshake” to “HTTP response”, via “TLS handshake”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Terminating TLS on every microservice without reason. Usually TLS ends at the edge/LB and mTLS is used internally only when needed.

questions.prompt: What main problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve?

choices.label: Many requests sharing one connection without waiting in line

questions.explanation: Multiple streams share one TCP connection.

questions.prompt: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Each version reduces connection overhead further.

questions.prompt: HTTP/3 transport?

choices.label: TCP. UDP gives unordered datagrams with no retransmits.
How long resolvers cache the record.
IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: QUIC over UDP.

title: DNS
objectives: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.
Answer: What does TTL control in DNS?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Browsers ask a recursive resolver, which walks root → .in/.com TLD → authoritative server and caches by TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover; high TTLs reduce lookups.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 6 steps from “Browser cache” to “IP”, via “Recursive resolver”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Forgetting that DNS caching delays failover. A 24 h TTL means some users hit the dead region for a day.

questions.prompt: Why lower a DNS TTL before a migration?

choices.label: So clients pick up the new IP faster

questions.explanation: Cached records expire sooner, so the switch propagates quickly.

questions.prompt: Order a cold DNS lookup.
questions.explanation: Resolution walks down the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: What does TTL control in DNS?

choices.label: p95 latency on the hot path plus error rate on writes/reads that affect revenue or safety.
N+1 queries and expensive nested queries.
How long resolvers cache the record.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: How long resolvers cache the record.

title: HTTP/HTTPS/TLS
objectives: Describe what TLS adds to HTTP
Count the round trips for a new HTTPS connection

cards.title: HTTPS in one sentence
cards.body: HTTPS is HTTP sent over a TLS-encrypted connection. TLS gives confidentiality (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and server authentication via a certificate chain.

cards.title: The handshake
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client hello (supported ciphers, key share)” to “Encrypted HTTP flows”, via “Server hello + certificate”.

cards.title: Where to terminate TLS
cards.body: Usually at the edge: a CDN or L7 load balancer decrypts, routes on the path, and talks to services over a private network (optionally re-encrypted with mTLS). Terminating close to the user cuts handshake latency.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Saying HTTPS makes an API secure. It protects data in transit only. You still need authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting.

questions.prompt: Your L7 load balancer must route /payments and /catalog to different services. Where should TLS terminate?

choices.label: At the load balancer (or edge), so it can read the HTTP path
Nowhere: send plain HTTP over the internet

questions.explanation: An L7 balancer can only route on paths it can read. Re-encrypt to services with mTLS if the internal network is not trusted.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HTTPS is accurate?

choices.label: It guarantees the server is fast
It removes the need for rate limiting
It protects data in transit but does not decide who may call your API

questions.explanation: Transport security and application security are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: A user in Chennai hits an origin in Singapore with about 60 ms RTT. Roughly how long before the first byte on a fresh TLS 1.3 connection (ignore DNS and server time)?

choices.label: About 120 ms: one RTT for TCP, one for TLS

questions.explanation: TCP handshake (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT) = about 2 × 60 ms before the request goes out.

flashcards.front: What three things does TLS provide?
Why terminate TLS at the edge?
flashcards.back: Shorter handshakes for users, and the L7 balancer can route on HTTP paths.
No. It protects data in transit; you still need AuthN and AuthZ.

title: REST API Design
objectives: Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs as actions, proper status codes, pagination and idempotency.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: GET /orders/42, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/42. Use 2xx/4xx/5xx correctly, cursor pagination for large lists, and versioning (/v1). PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not by default.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs as actions, proper status codes, pagination and idempotency.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client” to “201 Created + Location”, via “POST /v1/orders”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using verbs in URLs (/getOrder) and returning 200 with an error body. Status codes are part of the contract.

questions.prompt: Which method is idempotent by definition?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces the resource; repeating it has the same effect.

questions.prompt: Select good REST practices.
questions.explanation: GET must be safe — it should never mutate state.

questions.prompt: Idempotent methods?

choices.label: IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD (and OPTIONS).

flashcards.back: Cursor is stable and fast on large, changing lists.

objectives: GraphQL lets clients pick fields; gRPC gives fast typed RPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: GraphQL fits varied frontends that need different shapes from one endpoint. gRPC fits service-to-service calls: binary, schema-first, streaming, low latency.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using GraphQL without query cost limits — one nested query can fan out into thousands of DB calls (N+1).

title: Polling/Long Polling/SSE/WebSockets
objectives: Real-time options: polling, long polling, server-sent events (one-way), WebSockets (two-way).
Answer: How to route a message to a user on a different WS server?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Short polling wastes requests. Long polling holds a request open. SSE streams server→client over HTTP. WebSockets keep a full-duplex connection — needed for chat and live location.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Real-time options: polling, long polling, server-sent events (one-way), WebSockets (two-way).

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client opens WS” to “Push to client”, via “Gateway holds socket”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Ignoring connection state at scale: millions of sockets need dedicated gateway servers and a pub/sub to route messages to the right one.

questions.explanation: SSE is simple one-way streaming over HTTP.

questions.prompt: Which features need two-way real-time communication?
questions.explanation: Only interactive features need full-duplex sockets.

title: LB Algorithms
objectives: Round robin, least connections, weighted, and consistent hashing — pick by workload shape.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Round robin is simple for uniform requests. Least connections suits uneven request lengths. Weighted handles mixed hardware. Hashing (IP or key) gives affinity for caches.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Round robin, least connections, weighted, and consistent hashing — pick by workload shape.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Request” to “Update counters”, via “Algorithm”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using round robin when request durations vary wildly; slow servers accumulate a backlog.

questions.prompt: Requests vary from 5 ms to 5 s. Best default?
questions.explanation: It accounts for current load.

questions.prompt: Round robin vs Least connections: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Pick the algorithm that matches the workload.

choices.label: Let in-flight requests finish before removing a node.

title: L4 vs L7 LB & Health Checks
objectives: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 routes by HTTP content (paths, headers, cookies).

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: L4 forwards TCP/UDP connections without reading payloads. L7 terminates HTTP, so it can route /api vs /static, do header-based canary routing and TLS termination.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 routes by HTTP content (paths, headers, cookies).

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Packet arrives” to “Forward to pool”, via “L4: inspect IP/port”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Choosing L4 when you need path-based routing, or L7 for non-HTTP protocols.

questions.explanation: Only L7 understands HTTP paths.

questions.prompt: Path-based routing vs Raw TCP game server: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: L7 reads application data; L4 does not.

objectives: A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.
Answer: Reverse proxy sits in front of?
Answer: Forward proxy sits in front of?

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Nginx/Envoy as a reverse proxy hides backends, terminates TLS, compresses and caches. A forward proxy (corporate) sits in front of clients to filter or anonymise outbound traffic.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.

title: Stateless Services & Sessions
objectives: A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances and removes failed ones.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: LBs sit in front of a pool, run health checks, and route each request to a healthy backend. They enable horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys by draining instances.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances and removes failed ones.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client” to “Response”, via “Load balancer”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Forgetting the LB itself can fail. Run it as a redundant pair or use a managed, multi-zone LB.

choices.label: The LB stops sending it traffic

questions.explanation: Unhealthy targets are removed from rotation.

title: Where to Cache
objectives: Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Reads often follow a power law: a small set of keys gets most traffic. Serving them from memory (Redis, local LRU) drops latency from ms to µs and shields the DB.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 7 steps from “Request” to “Populate cache”, via “Check cache”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Caching everything blindly. Cache data that is read-heavy and tolerant of brief staleness.

questions.prompt: A 95% cache hit rate means:
questions.explanation: Only misses go to the database.

questions.prompt: 20K reads/s, 90% hit rate. How many reads/s reach the database?
assumptions: Use rounded daily volume ÷ 86,400 unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: Hit ratio formula?

choices.label: Many concurrent misses for one key overwhelm the DB.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: hits ÷ (hits + misses).

title: Cache Strategies
objectives: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and sets cache. Write-through: write cache and DB synchronously (fresh, slower writes). Write-behind: write cache, flush DB later (fast, risk of loss).

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Read cache” to “Return”, via “Miss”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using write-behind for payments. Losing buffered writes on a crash is unacceptable for money.

questions.prompt: Which risks data loss if the cache node crashes?
questions.explanation: DB writes are deferred.

questions.prompt: Cache-aside vs Write-through: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Each trades freshness, speed and safety differently.

questions.prompt: Most common strategy?

choices.label: Redis: data structures, persistence, replication; Memcached: simple multithreaded KV.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: Cache-aside (lazy loading).

objectives: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: LRU evicts least recently used — good default. LFU keeps frequently used items — good for stable hot sets. TTL expires data by age regardless of use.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: How a request flows

cards.title: Watch out for

cards.body: Stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB. Fix with request coalescing (single flight), locks, early refresh, and TTL jitter. Hot keys: replicate or add local caches.

title: CDN
objectives: CDNs cache static and media content close to users, cutting latency and origin load.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Edge PoPs cache assets with TTLs; misses go to origin. Use cache keys, versioned URLs for invalidation, and signed URLs for private media.
